analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal board that negotiates binding caps on what hospitals, doctors, and drug makers charge, and extends coverage to early retirees, strikers, and workers of failed businesses.
analysis.headline: The bill got hearings in a Senate Finance subcommittee in September 1991 but was never voted on in committee or on the floor, and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set up a Federal Health Expenditure Board to set national spending goals and force annual negotiations between health providers and the people who pay for care, with the results binding on hospitals, doctors, and drug companies. It would have created purchasing consortia in every state, let states adopt a single-payer health system with federal matching money, and extended coverage to early retirees, people on strike, and workers whose employers went out of business. It also rewrote the rules for small-employer health insurance, requiring community-style rating, guaranteed renewability, and standardized plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Early retirees too young for Medicare, workers on strike, and employees of companies that failed would gain public coverage. Workers at small businesses would gain from predictable, standardized premiums that could not be jacked up based on health status. All consumers would gain from lower health prices and public reports comparing providers on cost and quality.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Early retirees, strikers, and small-employer workers

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Federal Health Expenditure Board that sets national spending, access, and quality goals and convenes annual negotiations over payment rates for physician, hospital, and pharmaceutical services, with binding rates if the negotiators agree and Board-set rates if they do not.
Mandates uniform billing and claim forms and public annual reports on each provider's cost and effectiveness, to cut administrative waste and let consumers compare providers.

Lets any state set up a universal, single-payer health system financed by state taxes, with federal matching contributions equal to what the state would have gotten under the HealthAmerica Act's AmeriCare program.

Expands Medicare to retired people below the current eligibility age and covers early retirees not yet eligible, people on strike, and workers whose employers' businesses failed through the AmeriCare program in their state.

Rewrites small-employer insurance: carriers must offer the same plan to any small employer in the community, premiums must use a single rating system that stops treating groups differently based on health or risk, plans must be renewable on the same terms, and a toll-free number handles consumer complaints and helps small employers compare carriers.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, physicians, and pharmaceutical companies would bear the cost of negotiated, binding payment rates backed by civil fines for charging more. Health insurers would give up pricing freedom for small-employer plans and face standardized plan and disclosure requirements. Taxpayers would fund the new Board, state consortium grants, and expanded coverage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, doctors, drug makers, and insurers

drawbacks.text: The Board's negotiated rates are binding, and the bill imposes civil penalties — up to $500,000 for organizations in the Social Security Act version — on providers who charge, or purchasers who pay, other rates, a hard government price-control mechanism whose effects on innovation and access critics of rate-setting schemes contested.
Title V uses federal law to override state health-benefit mandates for these plans, preempting state consumer protections that some states had built up.
The uniform claims form requires a uniform patient identifier and mandatory reporting on every service, raising privacy concerns about a national database of individual care.
Large employer plans could be pulled under the new framework on an accelerated timetable, forcing a rapid restructuring of how employers buy health coverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks the two biggest problems patients faced in 1991 — rapidly rising prices and coverage that vanished when a job or pension did — with genuinely strong tools: binding negotiated rates, uniform billing to cut paperwork, and public provider report cards. The trade-offs are real: nationally negotiated price-setting was an untested mechanism in the U.S., enforcement relied on fines against providers, and the insurance title trampled state benefit mandates in the name of standardization. On balance it is a serious attempt at structural reform whose costs fall on the industries charging the high prices rather than on patients.

outcome.mechanism: After two September 1991 hearings in the Senate Finance Committee's health subcommittee, the bill sat in committee and never came up for a vote anywhere before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Paul Simon introduced the bill on August 2, 1991, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
The Finance Subcommittee on Health for Families held hearings on September 23 and concluded them September 30, 1991, with the hearings printed as S.Hrg. 102-462.
No committee vote, floor action, or further step followed; the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, physicians, drug manufacturers, and health insurers were better off because the bill died, since they never faced binding federal rate-setting or standardized small-employer insurance rules. The early retirees, strikers, and small-business workers the bill would have covered gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals, doctors, drug makers, and insurers

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; both sponsors were Democrats, and the bill died quietly in a committee chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: Hospitals would face Board-negotiated binding payment rates, with civil fines for charging anything else, and would submit audited financials and standardized billing data. Their resistance to rate-setting runs against patients' interest in lower prices.

Physician payment systems would be negotiated annually with the Board, and doctors charging other rates could face penalties. Patients benefit from contained fees but lose some physician autonomy over pricing.
Drug prices were one of the three sectors the Board was required to submit to binding negotiations, directly cutting into an industry that priced freely.

Carriers offering small-employer plans would lose underwriting freedom — single rating systems, standardized plans, guaranteed renewability, and audits — and small-share insurers would be enrolled into mandatory state purchasing consortia. Insurers' pricing latitude was part of what drove premiums up for small employers and sick people.
